question.leadin: Answer some questions about Roman Britain.
question.text: This structure marked the northern boundary of Roman Britain. It stretches across northern England and is named for the emperor who built it.
question.clue: A birthday invitation was found on one of the Vindolanda tablets, which were unearthed near this structure.

swap.text: This battle was a disastrous defeat of Hannibal by the Roman general Scipio Africanus. This battle was so detrimental to Carthage that it resulted in the immediate end of the Second Punic War.
swap.clue: The right wing of this battle was composed of cavalry under the direction of Massinissa.

question.leadin: To complete this siege, attacking forces built a wall around a hilltop fort, then built a wall around themselves to protect from a reinforcing army.
question.text: Name this 52 BCE siege of a hilltop fort commanded by Vercingetorix, whose surrender essentially guaranteed the fall of Gaul.
question.clue: A group of Mandubii civilians became trapped between the two sides of this battle and were left to starve.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about some of Rome's best emperors.
swap.text: This second of the group known as "the Five Good Emperors" expanded the Empire to its largest extent and is famous for his namesake column.
swap.clue: This man employed Apollodorus of Damascus to build a namesake forum as well as a bridge across the Danube.

question.leadin: This future emperor fell asleep during one of Nero's recitals and was exiled for a year.
question.text: Name this emperor, whose last words were "dear me, I think I'm becoming a god." This suppressor of the Great Jewish Revolt emerged victorious after the Year of the Four Emperors.
question.clue: On his deathbed, this emperor exclaimed "I think I'm becoming a god."Primus and Mucianus aided this ruler at the Second Battle of Bedriacum, helping him consolidate power over Vitellius.

swap.leadin: A letter to Tacitus that described an eruption of this volcano detailed the death of the admiral of the Misenum fleet.
swap.text: Name this mountain near the Bay of Naples, whose AD 79 eruption destroyed the nearby town of Herculaneum.
swap.clue: Artifacts excavated from towns next to this feature were confined to a Secret Museum due to their incredibly erotic content.

question.leadin: The largest ancient sculpture ever found was unearthed in one of these structures.
question.text: The Farnese Bull was discovered in one example of these buildings named for Caracalla. The caldarium was a room in this building, while the hypocausta were located beneath them.
question.clue: One example of these buildings in Britain was dedicated to the goddess Sulis, while examples of these buildings in Rome were named after Caracalla and Diocletian.

swap.text: This man served as an advisor to the emperor Titus after fighting against the Romans in the First Jewish-Roman War, an event he recounted in his The Jewish War.
swap.clue: Beginning with the Maccabean revolt and ending at Masada, this writer recounts the rise and downfall of his people in De Bello Judaico.

question.leadin: He built the Cloaca Maxima and acquired the Sibylline books, but his son's crime and his overbearing demeanor led to his overthrow by Lucius Brutus.
question.text: Name this last king of Rome, whose character was reflected in his cognomen.
question.clue: This ruler took refuge with Aristodemus of Cumae after a battle in which Castor and Pollux purportedly fought against him.

swap.leadin: Identify these other kings of Rome.
swap.text: After his son raped the noblewoman Lucretia, this last king of Rome was driven out in 509 BC by a mob led by Junius Brutus and was forced into exile in Etruria.
swap.answer: Tarquinius Superbus or Tarquin the Proud
swap.clue: This Roman king overthrew Servius Tullius and was himself deposed after his son Sextus raped Lucretia, leading her kinsmen to rebel.

question.leadin: Answer some questions about the lives of women in the Roman world.
question.text: One important religious position held exclusively by women was this group of female priests. They were held to be incorruptible, and tended to the sacred fire of the goddess of the hearth.
question.clue: Livy claimed that a traitorous member of this group was crushed by the shields of the Sabines and then thrown from the namesake Tarpeian Rock.

swap.leadin: The Creed of Ulfilas and Letter of Auxentius give us the clearest picture of this set of teachings.
swap.text: Name this heresy briefly exonerated by the Council of Jerusalem which was named after a priest opposed by Athanasius.
swap.clue: The emperor Constantius espoused this belief, leading to its further condemnation at the First Council of Constantinople.

question.text: Before fleeing to the Balearics, Mago was defeated at this battle near Seville by a concealed force of Romans under Scipio Africanus. The battle of Baecula and this battle ended Carthaginian power in Spain.
question.clue: This battle's victor unusually placed legions on the wings and auxiliaries in the centre, later creating a concave formation that mirrored a battle occurring ten years prior.

swap.leadin: This Roman defeated Archelaus in multiple engagements in the First Mithridatic War.
swap.text: Name this man who marched on Rome a second time and declared himself dictator following the death of his rival Marius.
swap.clue: This enemy of the populares was vital in defeating the Numidian king, Jugurtha, but his superior, Gaius Marius, controversially took credit for the victory.

question.text: This saint asked, "if Rome can perish, what can be safe?" in a letter written during the invasion. His letters to St. Marcella, who died in Rome during the sack, are the best known sources for her life.

swap.leadin: Suetonius records how a ruler of this region, Ptolemy, was executed by Caligula because his purple cloak drew the attention of the crowd when he entered a theatre.
swap.text: Name this region that, after its annexation by Claudius, was divided into the provinces of Tingitana and Caesariensis. Another king of this region, Bocchus I, betrayed his son-in-law, Jugurtha, to Sulla.
swap.answerHtml: Mauretania [accept Mauretania Tingitana and Mauretania Caesariensis; prompt on North Africa, Maghreb, Algeria, Morocco, or the Atlas Mountains by asking “what was the Roman name of the region?”]
swap.clue: It's not Egypt, but a man named Ptolemy was the last Roman client king of this region; its earlier client kings included the Numidian prince Juba II.

question.leadin: Answer the following about the period leading to the Law of the Twelve Tables.
question.text: Table Eight stipulates that "whoever is convicted of speaking false witness shall be flung from" this place, named for the legendary figure whom Titus Tatius bribed to gain entry to the Capitoline Hill.

swap.text: Gaius Pontius forced a trapped Roman army to pass under the yoke in this 321 BC "battle," a decisive moment in the Second Samnite War.
swap.clue: At this event, Lentulus encouraged the Romans with an account of his father's actions during the Gallic sack of Rome.

question.leadin: Answer the following about the pathetic career of co-emperor Lucius Verus.
question.text: Just a couple years into the Marcomannic Wars, Verus croaked of food poisoning at the start of this plague that ran from 165 to 180 AD, and is sometimes named in honor of Galen.

swap.leadin: When this man tried opposing one of Julius Caesar's bills, a crowd dumped feces on him and then broke his fasces, in a nice bit of linguistic humor.
swap.text: Name this man, the son-in-law to Cato the Younger, who served a consul alongside Caesar in 59 BCE and attempted to derail all legislation. He led later led Pompey's navy in the civil war against Caesar.
swap.clue: Supporters of one of this man's political opponents mocked him by referring to "Julius and Caesar" as the two consuls.
